Multispectral GFMs and an ImageNet ResNet-50 are equivalent within the margin on about half of them. Labels with random offsets cost the least at equal label quality. Under other decoder heads the verdicts mostly hold on FLAIR-2 and are decoder dependent on HLS Burn Scars. On four of five real label pairs the real label costs more than its matched simulated type. No choice of pretraining data makes an encoder consistently more robust, so the encoder is better chosen by its accuracy under imperfect labels.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 100 pages (15 pages main text and references, 85 pages appendix), 78 figures, 68 tables. Extended version including supplementary material

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ToWo-VTON: Take-Off Wear-On Virtual Try-On via Topology-aware Decoupling
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Virtual Try-On (VTON) aims to synthesize garment transfer without physical trials. Although recent methods perform well on upper-body garments, they still struggle in lower-body and full-body scenarios with complex occlusions and large silhouette changes. To address this limitation, we introduce ToWo (Take-Off Wear-On), a two-stage paradigm that decouples body structure estimation from garment synthesis. Take-Off first generates a tight-fitting body proxy that provides estimated structural guidance, and Wear-On then synthesizes the target garment conditioned on this prior. This decoupling reduces source-garment interference, supporting garment placement under substantial silhouette variations. Built on this paradigm, we propose ToWo-VTON, a unified topology-aware framework with structure-aware supervision. We construct the Body-Fitting DressCode (BFDC) dataset via body-aware diffusion and VLM-based filtering to provide body-proxy supervision across upper-, lower-, and full-body cases. We instantiate ToWo-VTON on both diffusion-based and MLLM-guided backbones. For diffusion-based models, we fine-tune on BFDC using the body proxy as the person input. For the MLLM-guided model, we use native backbone conditioning for the body proxy and target garment, and add Garment Boosting Attention (GBA) to preserve garment details. Experiments on VITON-HD and DressCode demonstrate improvements over the evaluated baselines, with KID reductions of 26.1% and 58.6% for diffusion-based and MLLM-guided implementations, respectively. The combined BFDC-training and Take-Off/Wear-On strategy also produces more coherent limb layouts and garment boundaries across the evaluated garment categories.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Quantization for Action, Execution for Deployment: Joint Precision and Execution Selection for World Action Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: World action models guide robots by predicting the effects of actions or generating commands from observations. A model may compare hundreds of candidate futures before acting, repeatedly reading weights that must fit in device memory. Post-training quantization reduces the number of bits used to store pretrained weights, but a smaller model is not necessarily a deployable one: temporary tensors can exceed graphics processing unit (GPU) memory limits, while even small prediction errors can change the selected action. This creates two coupled challenges: identifying bit assignments that preserve task performance and determining which of them meet real execution constraints, without exhausting costly task trials. We present PTQ4WAM, a framework for choosing layer-wise bit assignments and execution routes under memory, latency and task-evaluation budgets. Calibration measurements guide candidate proposals, optionally with a language model agent. We profile full-model routes on the GPU before spending task trials on feasible assignments. Fusing group rescaling and reading visual history in place can make an otherwise infeasible assignment deployable. Across 15 workloads from four model families, the median task score is 99.2% of the corresponding 32-bit floating-point (FP32) score. On fixed GPU replays, the median speedup over FP32 is 2.36 times and the median reduction in peak allocated memory is 71.5%. The code will be released soon.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Visual-RFT++: Extending Visual Reinforcement Fine-Tuning to Multimodal Tool Use
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) has recently become a central paradigm for advancing Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), as demonstrated by systems such as OpenAI's o3 and the R1 series. Despite significant progress in LLMs, how to leverage RFT to unify visual perception, step-by-step reasoning, and agentic tool use into one coherent training paradigm remains an open challenge. In this work, we present Visual Reinforcement Fine-Tuning++ (Visual-RFT++), a unified framework that extends RFT to both visual perception tasks and multimodal agentic workflows, enabling LVLMs to reason with images, act upon images, and evaluate their own outputs using verifiable reward. With Visual-RFT++, open-source LVLMs not only show significant gains on diverse visual perception tasks, but also acquire agentic abilities such as web searching for real-time information and code-based image manipulation (e.g., cropping, rotation, and analysis). Across visual perception tasks, including fine-grained classification, few-shot detection, reasoning grounding, and open-vocabulary detection, Visual-RFT++ delivers strong gains over SFT, including a +24.3 percentage points improvement in one-shot fine-grained classification and +21.0 percentage points on COCO's 4-shot setting and +15.4 percentage points on LVIS with around several hundred samples. To evaluate agentic behaviors, we introduce the Multimodal Agentic Tool Bench (MAT) with MAT-Search and MAT-Coding. Visual-RFT++ surpasses its baseline by +18.6 F1 / +13.0 EM percentage points on MAT-Coding and +10.3 F1 / +8.7 EM percentage points on MAT-Search. It also shows gains of 29.3 F1 and 25.9 EM percentage points on multi-hop QA benchmarks such as 2Wiki and HotpotQA, demonstrating strong cross-modal generalization. Visual-RFT++ introduces a data-efficient and reward-driven framework that strengthens both visual reasoning and agentic adaptability.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Our code is available at https://github.com/Liuziyu77/Visual-RFT

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Search-RSI: Expanding Search Worlds Along Multimodal Agents' Capability Frontier
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent issues the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($δ_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PhysAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Reliable Remote Heart Rate Estimation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables non-contact heart-rate estimation from facial videos, but its weak physiological signal is easily corrupted by motion, illumination changes, occlusion, skin-appearance variation, and device noise. Existing rPPG methods typically rely on a single model to directly predict heart rate or recover pulse waveforms, while different strong estimators may produce conflicting yet individually plausible candidates for the same video. To resolve these conflicts, we propose PhysAgent, an inference-time multi-agent candidate-verification framework. Unlike direct prediction approaches, PhysAgent neither trains a new base rPPG model nor asks Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to output heart rate directly. In contrast, it treats outputs from multiple base estimators as physiological hypotheses to be verified and uses a lightweight 4B MLLM, Qwen3-VL-4B, to drive multi-agent reasoning over video conditions, signal reliability, and candidate disagreement. A deterministic physiological verifier checks the fusion proposal, and a reproducible numerical fusion process produces the final heart rate. Experimental results on multiple public rPPG benchmarks show that PhysAgent improves fusion stability and reliability across different datasets and source-domain settings, while avoiding the irreproducibility and physiological inconsistency of direct MLLM prediction or unconstrained ensemble fusion. The code will be released soon.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: RLM: Learning Real-World Automotive Radar Perception through Language Supervision in Simulation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Radar supports perception at long range and under adverse weather and low visibility, making it an important sensing modality for autonomous driving. However, radar learning remains fragmented across task-specific architectures and objectives, while limited real-world annotations hinder the development of transferable representations. We present Radar Language Model (RLM), a framework for pretraining radar representations through spatial language supervision in simulation. By describing vehicle counts and their spatial arrangement, language provides a common supervisory signal for tasks with different prediction outputs. We construct over 800,000 radar-caption pairs from 110 hours of diverse simulated driving. We also introduce a new contrastive objective that incorporates spatial scene similarity into radar-language alignment, encouraging representations that capture the structure expressed in these descriptions. The resulting features support scene captioning, vehicle segmentation and bounding-box detection after supervised adaptation to RADIATE dataset. Experiments demonstrate improved count-based F1, IoU, and Dice over vanilla CLIP, alongside the highest mean detection AP50 among the evaluated baselines. Detection gains persist under limited real-world annotation budgets, supporting spatial-language pretraining as a practical route to reusable radar representations.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: OmniSenMo: A Unified Multisensory Language Model for Generalizable Human Motion Estimation, Understanding, and Prediction
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) estimate, understand, and predict human motion, but mainly from RGB cameras. Depth, LiDAR, mmWave, and WiFi complement RGB under poor lighting, through occlusions, and in privacy-sensitive applications, but existing multisensory models cover only some of these sensing tasks. Covering all of them from any sensor subset is challenging, since the tokens of heterogeneous sensors are semantically inconsistent and spatially misaligned, paired multisensory data are scarce, and the tasks need different temporal granularities. We present OmniSenMo, a multisensory language model that takes the human skeleton as a common reference for all sensors. Its skeleton-grounded motion representation turns each sensor into joint tokens, one per body joint, so that any sensor subset is fused joint by joint and expressed in the motion vocabulary that the language model learned from motion capture and text. We pretrain it on all five sensors generated by our multisensory simulator, and Multi-Granularity Observation gives each task the frames it needs. On a cross-action split of MM-Fi, the same model with all five sensors outperforms the models compared on each task, including LEO-Fuse in pose estimation (84.1 vs. 89.0 mm MPJPE) and HoloLLM in unseen-action recognition (69.2% vs. 42.8%). Even without RGB, it outperforms both methods that use RGB, and in a cross-dataset validation on XRF55, it recognizes unseen actions far better than HoloLLM.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Audio-Visual Rearrangement
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We introduce Audio-Visual Rearrangement (AVR), a novel task in which an agent hears a spoken request, retrieves a suitable object, and delivers it to the requesting user or an instruction-specified destination. AVR requires the agent to understand the spoken request and acoustically localize the speaker for delivery. To support this task, we construct a dataset covering three query types: explicit target specification, speaker-relative spatial references, and implicit user intent, spanning eight subtypes with diverse object selection and delivery requirements. Moreover, we propose a framework that integrates a motion-aware spatial audio module into an audio-visual large language model to encode spatial cues from the spoken request and update them as the agent moves. We further incorporate auxiliary supervision for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding through multitask instruction tuning to improve action prediction. Experiments establish baseline performance in both seen and unseen environments, laying the groundwork for future research on embodied intelligence and human-robot interaction. The code will be publicly available soon.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: GUI-Q: Task-Sensitive Granularity and Relation-Preserving Quantization for GUI Agents
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents enable automated interactions with mobile, web, and desktop interfaces. However, their large memory footprint and repeated model calls hinder deployment on resource-constrained devices, motivating post-training quantization (PTQ) without full retraining. Quantization can degrade GUI response accuracy and distort the instruction-vision affinities and local spatial relations needed for GUI target selection. Small coordinate errors can cause missed clicks, while early action errors can alter subsequent interface states and disrupt task execution. Local reconstruction error alone does not directly assess whether these responses and relations are preserved. We propose GUI-Q, a PTQ framework that targets response and relation preservation with 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16). Task-Sensitive Granularity Allocation (TSGA) allocates finer groups under a scale-byte budget by combining response sensitivity with the measured reduction in activation-weighted distortion. Relation-Preserving Symmetry Selection (RPSS) then selects symmetric or asymmetric grids to preserve instruction-vision affinities and local spatial relations in GUIs. Across three GUI-capable models, GUI-Q improves mean grounding TargetHit by 8.04 to 12.55 points over the strongest evaluated 4-bit configurations, while reducing static peak graphics processing unit (GPU) memory by 49.9% to 56.2% relative to bfloat16 (BF16). Fixed-output replay with packed 4-bit execution provides 1.7 to 2.8 times model-call speedups. The code will be released.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: UniAIDet: A Unified and Universal Benchmark for AI-Generated Image Content Detection and Localization
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: With the rapid proliferation of image generative models, the authenticity of digital images has become a significant concern. While existing studies have proposed various methods for detecting AI-generated content, current benchmarks are limited in their coverage of diverse generative models and image categories, often overlooking end-to-end image editing and artistic images. To address these limitations, we introduce UniAIDet, a unified and comprehensive benchmark that includes both photographic and artistic images. UniAIDet covers a wide range of generative models, including text-to-image, image-to-image, image inpainting, image editing, and deepfake models. Using UniAIDet, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of various detection methods and answer three key research questions regarding generalization capability and the relation between detection and localization. Our benchmark and analysis provide a robust foundation for future research.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PathStream: Towards Streaming Diagnostic Copilots for Whole-Slide Pathology
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Pathologists reach a diagnosis by integrating morphological evidence across regions and magnifications along viewing trajectories. Existing pathology AI rarely reflects this process: models predict from selected image regions, answer questions within fixed visual contexts, or navigate slides autonomously. We formalize pathologist-led streaming diagnosis, in which the pathologist controls navigation while a copilot selectively describes incoming views and synthesizes accumulated evidence into a final diagnosis. We record five pathologists' viewing trajectories on 1,791 TCGA whole-slide images (WSIs) spanning ten organs, with response labels, morphological descriptions, and session-level findings and diagnoses. We construct PathStreamBench to assess response timing, morphological description, and session-level diagnosis, alongside auxiliary video understanding. We introduce PathStream, which jointly learns streaming responses and diagnosis through two-stage training, with a diagnosis-attention loss guiding attention during diagnosis to relevant visual and textual evidence accumulated as the examination unfolds. PathStream outperforms 14 vision-language models and three domain-fine-tuned baselines on the core tasks, achieving a trajectory WSI Relevance score of 77.87, surpassing the strongest domain-fine-tuned baseline's 62.76. Without additional training, its diagnostic capabilities generalize to new educational pathology videos, three external centers, and an unseen organ.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Multimodal View Training: Learning More Through Different Modalities
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Can a language model learn more from the same information simply by encountering it in different forms? We answer this in the affirmative by introducing Multimodal View Training (MVT), a simple training approach that presents identical information through text, speech, and images, without requiring new facts or supervision. Starting from a text sample, MVT generates corresponding audio and rendered-text image views, and trains a multimodal language model to produce the same target output across all three views. To further bring these benefits to text-only large language models (LLMs), we train lightweight connector modules to pretrained audio and vision encoders, allowing the LLM to learn from multimodal inputs while retaining its text-only architecture at inference. Across question answering, machine unlearning, and knowledge editing, adaptive MVT improves QA recall by +15.2 percentage points, forget quality by +40.7 points, and editing generality by +25.2 points over text-only training. Combining MVT with standard augmentation further improves QA and editing generality. Our theoretical analysis illustrates how training across modalities can shift weight updates toward shared factual content and reduce their reliance on features specific to each view.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: WaDiS: Boundary-Preserving Diffusion Segmentation via Multi-Scale Wavelet Conditioning and Frequency-Aware Gating
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Diffusion models have shown strong potential in medical image segmentation due to their generative capabilities and robustness. However, existing methods often struggle to preserve fine anatomical boundaries and to retain multi-scale structural information due to the loss of spatial and frequency details during feature encoding, particularly in complex clinical imaging conditions. This work presents WaDiS, a wavelet-powered conditional latent diffusion framework for medical image segmentation that addresses these limitations through multi-scale wavelet conditioning and frequency-aware information filtering for boundary preservation. The model adopts a multi-scale wavelet conditioning encoder to retain rich structural features, leveraging its lossless nature to better preserve semantic priors critical to the diffusion process. In addition, a Frequency-Aware Gating Block (FAGB) is introduced into the skip connections of the diffusion U-Net, enabling adaptive spectral filtering and residual fusion to better emphasize boundary structures while reducing irrelevant content. To improve generalization across clinical domains, we adopt a structure-preserving color augmentation strategy during training. Specifically, global color statistics are transferred between samples in the LAB color space, allowing the model to decouple appearance from structure and focus more on anatomical shape rather than color bias. Experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that WaDiS consistently outperforms existing diffusion-based and conventional segmentation methods, with notable improvements in boundary accuracy, robustness to noise, and generalization under color variation. The code for this work will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: OpenViVE: New Benchmark and Dual-Stream Co-Attention Framework for Vietnamese Visual Entailment
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Visual Entailment (VE) determines whether a textual hypothesis is entailed, contradicted, or unverifiable from an image. However, existing VE benchmarks are largely English-centric and do not capture Vietnamese-specific linguistic distinctions or culturally grounded visual contexts. To address this gap, we introduce OpenViVE, the first large-scale native Vietnamese VE benchmark, containing 62,268 balanced image-hypothesis pairs from 10,378 culturally grounded images. OpenViVE is constructed using an Artifact-Aware Hybrid LLM-Human Pipeline that combines constrained generation, human validation, and PMI-guided refinement. The pipeline substantially reduces hypothesis-only shortcuts, with Contradiction accuracy dropping from 96% to 66% after artifact refinement. We further evaluate a dual-stream PhoBERT-ConvNeXt framework with bidirectional co-attention to align visual evidence with Vietnamese hypotheses. The framework achieves 84.84% accuracy and 84.90% macro-F1 on the test set, while PhoBERT consistently outperforms multilingual XLM-R variants. These results highlight the importance of language-specific encoding and explicit cross-modal interaction for Vietnamese VE.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: UUBench: Understanding the Unspoken toward Full-Duplex Multimodal Interaction
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Effective real-time, full-duplex multimodal interaction requires systems to understand not only what users say, but also the communicative needs conveyed through prosody, facial expressions, gestures, and context, and to generate audiovisual responses that appropriately address those needs. Existing evaluations offer limited insight into whether systems translate an understanding of such unspoken needs into effective responses. We introduce UUBench, a benchmark for assessing how well multimodal interactive systems Understand the Unspoken intent and address users' implicit communicative needs. The inherent subjectivity of implicit intent inference poses a key challenge for evaluation. To address this, we introduce Process-Oriented Scoring, which grounds the assessment of intent fulfillment in observable auditory and visual cues, such as prosody and gestures. Rather than relying solely on a single overall score, it evaluates how well a response addresses the communicative needs conveyed by each applicable primitive dimension. We aggregate the dimension-level scores according to each dimension's relevance to the annotated evidence. Beyond intent fulfillment, Outcome-Oriented Scoring evaluates the naturalness, appropriateness, and human-likeness of the reply itself under audio-only, visual-only, and audiovisual conditions. To make these judgments traceable to observable evidence, we propose a Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV module, which uses structured, timestamped audiovisual observations of the user and the digital human's reply to assess one dimension or criterion at a time. UUBench provides a foundation for assessing whether multimodal interactive systems respond effectively to meaning beyond literal wording, supporting progress toward context-aware, real-time, full-duplex interaction.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 49 pages, 37 figures, 9 tables, including appendices. Preview version; work in progress

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Preserve to Compress: Beyond Low-Dimensional Latents in One-Step Diffusion Codec
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Pretrained latent diffusion models bring powerful generative priors to ultra-low-bitrate image compression, but their latent spaces reflect a reconstruction--generation tradeoff. Low-dimensional latents reduce modeling cost but can discard image details, while higher-dimensional latents improve reconstruction yet make diffusion optimization harder under a fixed computational budget. Generative codecs that adopt these pretrained spaces also inherit this compromise, even though compression requires fidelity to a specific source image. In particular, low-dimensional latent interfaces can discard source details before coding and restrict how much decoded information reaches the image decoder. We propose Preserving Information for Compression and Synthesis (PICS), a one-step generative image compression framework that adapts these interfaces to preserve source information. Our Information-Preserving Adaptors (IPAs) expose richer features for coding and retain decoded information throughout reconstruction, while deferred decoder adaptation stabilizes training and helps the image decoder exploit the expanded representations. Experiments on Kodak, DIV2K, and CLIC 2020 show average BD-rate savings of 52.64% and 39.61% over StableCodec at matched LPIPS and DISTS, respectively.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CoRE: Weakly Supervised Coarse-to-Fine Risk Evidence Learning in Driving Videos
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Driver perceived risk evolves in dynamic environments and is supported by specific scene entities, yet supervision is typically limited to coarse video-level judgments. Learning when supporting evidence emerges and which entities support a risk predictor would require costly temporal- and entity-level annotations. We introduce CoRE, a weakly supervised coarse-to-fine framework that learns fine-grained prediction support from coarse video supervision. CoRE trains and freezes a video-level predictor. Structured interventions over candidate temporal regions or entity tracks measure how each candidate changes the coarse prediction, producing graded prediction-effect targets. These targets are distilled into a student that directly predicts temporal and entity support from the original video, without interventions at inference. We evaluate this learning principle across three complementary settings. RISEE tests perceived-risk support from subjective clip-level judgments without temporal or entity-level risk annotations. DoTA provides independent temporal event annotations for evaluating weakly supervised traffic-anomaly localization. UCF-Crime tests whether the same coarse-to-fine mechanism extends to a standard non-driving anomaly-detection benchmark. Across these settings, CoRE learns informative fine-grained support from coarse supervision, with strong temporal localization on DoTA and competitive performance on UCF-Crime. These results establish coarse video predictions as supervision for recovering the fine-grained evidence supporting them, without corresponding fine-grained labels.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: LeadVLA: Learning Follower-Aware Route Execution for Robot Leading
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SIGNTOK: A Text-Aligned Continuous Pose Tokenizer for Sign Language Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Text-conditioned sign language generation (SLG) depends not only on the generator but also on the space in which signing is generated. Existing approaches generate directly in pose space, in quantized code spaces, or in learned latent spaces trained for reconstruction. We find that these spaces are organized largely by signer identity rather than linguistic content: on CSL-Daily, a test clip's nearest neighbor in raw pose space is the same sentence signed by another person in only 2% of cases. To address this, we propose SIGNTOK, a continuous pose tokenizer whose latent space is shaped by three training-only heads: a kinematics head that predicts motion dynamics, a sentence-level head that aligns signing with the overall text, and a word-level head that aligns short motion windows with content words. Together, these objectives raise the same-sentence cross-signer nearest-neighbor rate to 82%. On three sign language benchmarks, the same generator trained in the SIGNTOK latent instead of pose space raises back-translation BLEU-4 in five of six benchmark-scorer settings at comparable joint accuracy, and word-level alignment gives higher back-translation scores than sentence-level alignment on every benchmark.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: UniWorld-View: Large-Baseline View Synthesis via Video Diffusion Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Novel view synthesis from casually captured monocular images and videos offers a practical route to immersive content creation without dedicated multi-view capture. However, the limited viewpoint coverage of such inputs leaves scene geometry insufficiently constrained, restricting the ability of reconstruction-based methods, such as neural radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), to render views far from the observed viewpoints. Generative approaches leverage learned visual priors to synthesize unobserved content, but maintaining geometric consistency and precise camera control remains challenging under large viewpoint changes. We present UniView, a unified framework for large-baseline novel view synthesis and scene generation from monocular images and videos. Central to our approach are an occlusion-aware point cloud renderer and a dual-branch conditioning mechanism. The renderer uses triple reprojection to identify and filter unreliable projections under large viewpoint changes. The conditioning mechanism integrates the resulting geometric guidance with source-view appearance within the video diffusion model, enabling precise camera control while preserving visual details and synthesizing unobserved content. To extend view synthesis to scene generation, we introduce a two-stage generation strategy that decouples viewpoint changes from temporal evolution. This strategy produces dense, synchronized multi-view videos that provide additional supervision for dynamic Gaussian Splatting, enabling more complete 4D generation from monocular observations. Extensive evaluations across static and dynamic scenes demonstrate the effectiveness of UniView in novel view synthesis and scene generation, combining precise camera control with geometric consistency and visual fidelity.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MemOVCD: Training-Free Open-Vocabulary Change Detection via Cross-Temporal Memory Reasoning and Global-Local Adaptive Rectification
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Open-vocabulary change detection (OVCD) seeks to identify semantic changes in bi-temporal remote sensing imagery with text-specified target categories. Representative foundation-model pipelines decode the two timestamps independently before comparing their predictions, leaving cross-temporal evidence unavailable to semantic decoding. Moreover, current patch-wise inference can undermine global semantic continuity, yielding fragmented predictions. To address these limitations, we put forward MemOVCD, a training-free framework which reformulates OVCD as cross-temporal memory-conditioned inference. Specifically, MemOVCD casts bi-temporal analysis as a bidirectional two-frame tracking problem and exploits the memory mechanism of video SAM to propagate semantic candidate regions across timestamps. Their features are pooled and averaged into a local exemplar token. Subsequently, a shared memory, whose number of prototypes is determined by local-exemplar availability, aggregates regional features from the unlabeled target collection. The local and shared tokens are then jointly used to condition the subsequent semantic segmentation. We further devise a global-local adaptive rectification strategy, which adaptively fuses local and global predictions to compensate for incomplete spatial support when processing large images while preserving fine-grained details. MemOVCD and its inductive variant L-MemOVCD show favorable performance on five benchmarks, and ablations and analyses further validate its effectiveness under evaluated settings. Our code will be publicly available.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Code will be released in: https://github.com/kzigzag/MemOVCD

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: T-VSS: Test-Time Visual Subspace Steering for Adversarial Robustness of Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Contrastive vision-language models (VLMs), exemplified by CLIP, enable strong zero-shot visual recognition but remain highly vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. Recent test-time adaptation methods improve robustness without retraining. Prompt-based methods adapt learnable text prompts, while input-space methods optimize pixels or padding at test time. These approaches can improve predictions, but they do so through an indirect and expensive optimization path. We propose \textbf{Test-time Visual Subspace Steering (T-VSS)}, a lightweight defense that performs test-time adaptation directly in the visual feature space. T-VSS first builds a sample-specific low-rank subspace from multi-view feature residuals anchored at the attacked image. It then learns a shared feature correction within this subspace using reliability-weighted entropy minimization. By constraining adaptation to a compact visual geometry, T-VSS steers attacked features toward more stable and discriminative predictions while avoiding noisy full-space updates. Experiments on fine-grained, ImageNet, and ImageNet-OOD benchmarks show that T-VSS improves adversarial robustness while maintaining competitive clean accuracy and better efficiency than prior test-time adaptation methods. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/jhyukjang/T-VSS}{here}.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: RMR-VLA: Recurrent Memory Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation often requires acting on visual cues that have disappeared, such as an object indicated earlier or a target hidden under a moving cup. The key challenge is to maintain what past evidence means for the next action as the scene changes. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), an explicit reasoning step that connects memory to action inside a vision-language-action model (VLA), with no external reasoning model. At each update, the VLA first infers an event from visual evidence, then revises the task state and grounds a subgoal in the current scene to guide action generation. Carrying the state and subgoal across updates lets remembered identities and task progress determine the current target, doubling RoboMME success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence. Joint training lets one VLA both reason and act; because its memory decisions are text tokens with exact likelihoods, GRPO refines them from rollout rewards without making action generation stochastic. Among the compared methods, RMR-VLA achieves the best results on RoboMME (66.46% overall, 79.83% on the Reference category) and LIBERO-Mem (90.08%).

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Tripwire: Robot Agents that Program Their Own Interrupts under Human Disturbance
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Agent harnesses are turn-based: the agent acts, waits for the result, then reasons. When the action invokes a pretrained robot policy, such as a vision-language-action (VLA) or world action model (WAM), the policy may react continuously to observations, but the agent cannot revisit its decision until the call returns. Meanwhile, a person may step into the robot's path or move the object it is about to grasp. Invoking the agent more often narrows this blind interval, but a reasoning model takes seconds per decision and most control steps need no new one. We propose TRIP, a training-free, event-driven harness in which the agent programs its own interrupts. With each call, the agent writes a tripwire: a lightweight, stateful Python program that runs alongside the policy, can query a compact VLM (for example, to locate a person and measure their distance), and decides whether the call continues or control returns to the agent. When it fires, the harness halts the policy and returns control with the reason; the agent then reassesses, adapts, and continues under a rewritten tripwire. We evaluate TRIP with three VLAs and one WAM on RoboHD, a benchmark of 168 RoboCasa365 scenes in which a simulated person disturbs the robot and any human-robot contact counts as failure. Compared with a turn-based harness using the same agent and tools, TRIP halves the rate of human contact with the strongest policy, raising safety from 61.3% to 81.3%, without sacrificing task success (38.7% vs. 31.0%). Real-robot experiments show that TRIP completes two manipulation tasks under human interference where the turn-based harness and the policy alone largely fail.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Separating Protocol Effects from Spatio-Temporal Evidence in Person Re-Identification Re-Ranking
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Spatio-temporal priors re-rank person re-identification matches using the camera pair and the time gap, and are reported to add large gains on Market-1501. We ask how much of such a gain encodes the evaluation protocol rather than learned spatio-temporal evidence. Starting from a course-project re-ranker that adds log camera-transition and log time-gap terms to cosine similarity, we train a strong ResNet-50 baseline (Rank-1 94.3 %, mAP 86.2 % over three seeds), choose the fusion weights on an identity-disjoint validation split and evaluate on the official test set with control priors. The repository form adds 2.30 mAP points, but a one-parameter penalty on same-camera pairs alone adds 2.19: the protocol never places a true match in the query's camera, so the penalty removes distractors for free. The time term of that form is almost unused; a pair-level diagnostic traces this to its modelling the time gap given a match without dividing by the gap distribution of all candidate pairs. A likelihood-ratio prior adds 4.04 points without the penalty and 5.62 with it; shuffling the time stamps removes the extra gain, so about 3.43 points are tied to identity. The prior fixes the first-ranked match of 4.2 % of the queries and breaks it for 0.1 %. The gain shrinks as the visual baseline improves (11.9 to 5.62 points between a 70.5 % and a 86.2 % mAP model) and concentrates on queries whose true matches share the query's video sequence. The study covers one dataset, one backbone and three seeds.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ObjectTwin: Training-Free Asset Verification for Captured Scenes
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: An editable digital twin needs assets that faithfully represent the particular objects captured. Partial observations leave both unseen geometry and asset placement uncertain: several registrations can explain the available views while predicting different surfaces elsewhere. We introduce ObjectTwin, a training-free framework for capture-conditioned asset verification. It retains calibration-compatible alignments, checks observed surfaces and known free space, and carries the resulting range of evidence into acceptance, exclusion, or deferred inspection. Withheld observations evaluate each fixed decision. Across Replica and ScanNet, capture correspondence improves held-out asset selection over registered geometry, reducing mean IoU regret by 55% on shared candidate pairs. Across multiview reconstruction, amodal completion, and scene generation, surface-based selection identifies the best unseen-view candidate for 97.5% of shared test objects. Controlled edits verify sensitivity to visible errors and invariance to unobserved geometry. Compatible alignments also predict different unseen outcomes, while strong single-fit controls distinguish this sensitivity from gains in screening accuracy. Together, these experiments establish capture correspondence as a useful asset-selection signal and provide a reproducible framework for evaluating absolute quality and alignment-dependent decisions.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 30 pages, 20 figures, 22 tables; includes supplementary material. Expanded and retitled: training-free asset verification, held-out selection, alignment analysis, and additional reconstruction methods. Project page: https://styokuok.github.io/sim_ready/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: TPGDiff: Hierarchical Triple-Prior Guided Diffusion for Image Restoration
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: All-in-one image restoration aims to address diverse degradation types using a single unified model. Existing methods typically rely on degradation priors to guide restoration, yet often struggle to reconstruct content in severely degraded regions. Although recent works leverage semantic information to facilitate content generation, integrating it into the shallow layers of diffusion models often disrupts spatial structures (\emph{e.g.}, blurring artifacts). To address this issue, we propose a Triple-Prior Guided Diffusion (TPGDiff) network for unified image restoration. TPGDiff incorporates degradation priors throughout the diffusion trajectory, while introducing structural priors into shallow layers and semantic priors into deep layers, enabling hierarchical and complementary prior guidance for image reconstruction. Specifically, we leverage multi-source structural cues as structural priors to capture fine-grained details and guide shallow layers representations. To complement this design, we further develop a distillation-driven semantic extractor that yields robust semantic priors, ensuring reliable high-level guidance at deep layers even under severe degradations. Furthermore, a degradation extractor is employed to learn degradation-aware priors, enabling stage-adaptive control of the diffusion process across all timesteps. Extensive experiments on both single- and multi-degradation benchmarks demonstrate that TPGDiff achieves superior performance and generalization across diverse restoration scenarios. Our project page is: https://leoyjtu.github.io/tpgdiff-project.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: AxE: Benchmarking Agent-Environment Generalization of Video World Models via Grounded Events
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Edge cases are not the long tail; they are the norm. An embodied system deployed across changing environments, bodies, objects, and tasks will routinely encounter combinations that were absent from its training data. General-purpose physical intelligence therefore requires world models that reuse prior knowledge, predict consequences, and adapt with little or no additional training. Yet current evaluations of conditional video generation emphasize visual quality, prompt alignment, or isolated physical plausibility, leaving systematic generalization difficult to measure. We introduce AxE Bench, a benchmark that organizes condition changes along eight factors of the acting agent and of its environment, and pairs every original condition with controlled variants that change one side or both. WBench-plus applies the same structure to an existing multi-turn benchmark, pairing each WBench scenario with variants on the environment side, through its world setting or camera behavior, or on the agent side, through its interaction instructions. Additionally, to score generated futures, we develop an evaluation harness that combines vision-language reasoning with targeted computer-vision evidence, converting each video into temporally localized events and comparing generated events with reference events in both time and semantics. We summarize each model with the AxE Score, event Fidelity weighted by its Stability across original-variant pairs. Across twenty models, generated events match reference events far more often in timing than in content: no model exceeds a Fidelity of 13.01, the highest Stability is 0.55, and the highest AxE Score is 7.10. Together, these components turn world-model generalization from an informal aspiration into a falsifiable evaluation program for real and simulated interactions. Our project website can be found at: AxEBench.github.io

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: What Remains After Concept Erasure? Sparse Autoencoder Probes for Auditing Diffusion Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Concept erasure aims to remove selected visual concepts from text-to-image diffusion models while preserving the generation of non-target concepts. Evaluation typically measures target suppression and non-target preservation in generated images, but a concept's absence from these outputs does not establish its removal from the model. We introduce SAE-Audit, a white-box audit using sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes to test whether activation interventions can restore target-concept generation without changing model weights or test prompts. After verifying target suppression, we compare the original and edited models using a shared SAE representation learned from original-model activations, identifying features whose target-related responses weaken after erasure. We inject sparse directions derived from the original-model responses into the edited model, keeping these directions fixed across test prompts, and evaluate recovery on held-out scene families. Experiments span six erasure methods and four domains: objects, artistic styles, copyrighted content, and nudity. Interventions using a few dozen selected SAE features yield higher average recovery rates than matched random-feature interventions, with recovery concentrated in objects and nudity following cross-attention edits. Most styles and copyrighted concepts show limited recovery under the tested intervention settings. These findings show that output suppression can coexist with responsiveness to sparse concept directions supplied from the original model.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Thermal-Guided Low-Light UAV Image Enhancement: A Reliability-Aware Guidance Network and a Unified Benchmark
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Thermal-guided low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is promising for nighttime unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) perception because thermal imagery remains informative under severe visible degradation. However, the degraded visible image serves as both the alignment reference and the enhancement target, making thermal guidance uncertain in its spatial correspondence and local utility under low illumination, sensor differences, and UAV motion. Misaligned or unsuitable thermal cues may introduce artifacts, while spatially varying degradation requires region-specific restoration rather than uniform enhancement. To address these challenges, we propose a Reliability-Aware Multi-Strategy Guidance Network (RMGNet) for thermal-guided UAV LLIE under weak optical-thermal alignment. Its Reliability-Aware Guidance Calibration Module (RAGCM) performs coarse-to-fine displacement estimation and jointly evaluates the reliability of aligned thermal guidance and the usability of degraded visible evidence. Based on calibrated guidance, degradation, and reliability cues, the Multi-Strategy Enhancement Routing Module (MSERM) generates candidates for detail preservation, highlight-protected relighting, and thermal compensation, then spatially routes their contributions. We further construct the UAV weakly aligned Optical-Thermal dataset (UWOT), the largest UAV-oriented benchmark to date for weakly aligned optical-thermal low-light enhancement, containing 5,000 triplets. Extensive experiments show that RMGNet outperforms representative single-modal and multimodal state-of-the-art methods in enhancement quality while retaining competitive computational efficiency and greater robustness to practical cross-modal misalignment. The dataset and code will be publicly available at https://github.com/mmic-lcl/Datasets-and-benchmark-code.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Let It Be Simple: One-Step Action Generation for Vision-Language-Action Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: One-step generation from standard diffusion or Flow-Matching training is rarely effective for text-to-image or video generation without distillation or specialized one-step objectives. We find that VLA action generation behaves strikingly differently. Biasing only the training timestep distribution toward the noise endpoint yields strong one-step policies across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and real-world robot tasks. Moreover, for open-source VLA models with different architectures, simply replacing iterative decoding with a single forward pass often performs comparably to the original multi-step decoding on benchmarks such as LIBERO, CALVIN, and SimplerEnv. We attribute this difference to the condition-target structure of VLA generation, which is closer to image-to-text than text-to-image: rich observations strongly constrain a comparatively compact target. We formalize this intuition through the irreducible velocity loss $R_v(t,c)$ of standard Flow Matching, which becomes much smaller toward the noise endpoint for VLA, whereas image-generation models usually exhibit a U-shaped profile. The geometry induced by the learned generative map shows the same contrast: the Jacobian of this map with respect to the initial noise has a substantially smaller largest singular value for action generation than for image generation. Together, these results suggest that VLA's condition-target structure makes one-step generation unusually accessible to standard Flow Matching. Code and training configurations for this paper are available at https://github.com/bondtesty/let-it-be-simple.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: AVIS: Adaptive Test-Time Scaling for Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) benefit from chain-of-thought prompting and test-time scaling, but these gains often come with prohibitive inference cost due to large visual contexts and long decoding chains. We view this cost through two coupled axes: Visual Context Scaling (VCS), which controls how much visual evidence is passed to the language model, and Visual Reasoning Scaling (VRS), which controls how much inference-time reasoning search is performed. Existing methods typically optimize one axis at a time, leaving the joint allocation of compute across these axes underexplored. We introduce Adaptive Visual Inference Scaling (AVIS), a lightweight policy that adapts both VCS and VRS per query. AVIS realizes VCS through Key Diversity Visual (KDV) pruning, a training-free $O(N)$ key-based rule for removing redundant visual tokens before prefilling, and realizes VRS through adaptive self-consistency, using a learned difficulty predictor to select the number of reasoning rollouts. AVIS is deployment-friendly and compatible with shared-prefill inference, where all rollouts reuse a single prefilling pass and KV cache. Across diverse image and video reasoning benchmarks, AVIS improves the accuracy--compute trade-off relative to VCS-only and VRS-only baselines, and remains effective on top of RL post-trained VLMs while keeping compute and latency low.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: LMnOP: Pruning 3D Gaussian Splatting via Leave-Many-Out Importance
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting renders photorealistic views in real time. However, a single scene often needs millions of Gaussians, so these models are costly to store and render. Pruning reduces this cost by keeping a subset of the Gaussians. A common score is the leave-one-out importance, which is the loss increase when a Gaussian alone is removed. At high pruning ratios, many Gaussians are removed together, so Gaussians that are redundant alone but essential together are lost. We present LMnOP (Leave-Many-Out Pruning), which estimates the importance of each Gaussian under the removal of the other Gaussians. This leave-many-out importance is the average loss increase when a Gaussian is removed while the others are also removed at random. We compute the exact mean and variance of each pixel's color under random removal in closed form, and approximate the importance from them without sampling removal patterns. We refine each Gaussian's probability of remaining with its importance and prune once at the end. Without fine-tuning, LMnOP achieves the best results in 16 of 18 metrics on three datasets at 90% and 99% removal. It improves SSIM and LPIPS over GaussianPOP in all 13 scenes.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Agent on Guard: Self-Improving Runtime Intervention for Robust Robotic Manipulation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Robot foundation policies provide learned execution capabilities, while programming agents can reason about failures and construct recovery behaviors. Combining them effectively requires learning when intervention helps and when the policy can reliably resume. This challenge is inherently temporal: the physical world continues to evolve during reasoning, and a useful recovery may become infeasible before a decision takes effect. We introduce Agent on Guard (AoG), a hierarchical framework that improves collaboration between a frozen base policy and a programming agent through physical experience. An evolving outer planner allocates control as the physical state evolves, aligning decisions with the physical clock with attention to observation freshness, remaining recovery windows, and the time required for reasoning, recovery, and subsequent execution. Coupled inner loops jointly refine intervention timing, recovery skills, and handoff conditions. Rather than judging recovery by local correction alone, AoG uses downstream task progress, failure recurrence, final outcomes, and resource consumption to improve both recovery behaviors and scheduling. This turns temporary agent solutions into reusable collaboration capabilities that complement the frozen policy. On RoboDojo-Sim, AoG achieves a success rate of 50.57% and a task score of 57.26, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 11.22 percentage points and 10.68 points, respectively. It also reduces end-to-end episode latency by 80.4% and online token consumption by 85.1% relative to the GPT-6 Astra agent.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Policy-intrinsic Demonstration Curation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Fine-tuning a robot policy for a new target task requires target demonstrations, but only a few are available. Demonstrations of other tasks can fill this gap, and demonstration curation selects the useful ones among these candidates. Retrieval-based curation selects the candidates that are most similar to the target demonstrations. Since it does not use the policy, any candidate that looks similar receives a high score. Performance-aware curation therefore estimates the effect of each candidate on the policy. However, this requires training on the candidates and takes a long time. We propose a third branch, policy-intrinsic curation, which uses the policy and still takes little time. It estimates this effect with forward passes of the pretrained policy and needs no training. We instantiate this branch with PICKER (Policy-Intrinsic Curation from Known Errors). It selects the candidates on which the policy makes errors that agree with those on the target demonstrations. PICKER reaches success rates comparable to those of performance-aware curation and takes about as long as retrieval-based curation. Its selection is also stable across seeds.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 15 pages (including 1 page of references and 6 pages of appendices), 5 figures, 7 tables

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: GraspHOI: Full-Body 3D Human-Object Reconstruction with Finger-Level Grasps from a Single In-the-Wild Image
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Existing monocular full-body 3D human-object interaction (HOI) methods do not combine category-agnostic object reconstruction with finger-level contact. Their hands may float off or sink into objects, breaking realism in AR/VR environments. We present GraspHOI, the first category-agnostic framework that reconstructs a full-body 3D HOI from a single image and jointly refines the arms and fingers so that the hands meet the reconstructed object surface. GraspHOI reconstructs the body, hands, and object separately with foundation models and places them in a shared metric camera frame through depth-based registration and silhouette alignment. Occlusion-aware contact correspondences seat the object against the hand, and contact-aware optimization refines shoulder, elbow, wrist, and finger rotations while anchoring the joints to the image. We find that with fingers capped near the image estimate, refining them alone is insufficient; freeing the arm removes most of the remaining hand-object gap, since in a full body the arm chain places the hand. In experiments on three datasets, GraspHOI yields more plausible hand-object contact than four baselines and better relative human-object placement than HDM and TeHOR.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: When "A or B" Is Less Likely than A: Coherent Probabilities for Vision Decision Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision decision models answer a multiple-choice question about an image with one probability per option, and software uses them directly. We show that the probabilities depend on how the options are grouped: a merged option "A or B" receives on average 11.5 points less probability than the sum of A and B. This under-additivity appears at every model size from 0.85B to 26B and remains after fine-tuning on labels. We propose CORE, which asks each training question with its options regrouped and trains the answers to all these questions toward one target distribution over the original options, summed into each question's groups. On 1,050 items from seven benchmarks, CORE reduces the total variation distance between the answer to a regrouped question and the original answer summed into the same groups from 14.8 to 5.8 points on the 0.85B model, against 9.4 for the best baseline trained on the same questions. At all five model sizes, CORE reduces this distance without lowering accuracy.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: RadarOSV: Unified 3D Scene and Motion Perception from mmWave Radars
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Millimeter-wave radar offers weather-resilient sensing for 3D occupancy prediction. Existing radar occupancy methods mainly model geometry, with limited joint modeling of semantics and motion. Cascaded imaging radar provides fine spatial detail but has a limited unambiguous velocity range, whereas single-chip radar offers a wider range but coarser spatial resolution. We propose RadarOSV, to our knowledge the first radar-only framework that jointly predicts occupancy, dynamic object semantics, and ground-relative velocity from raw radar data in unified voxels, by exploiting complementary measurements from both radars. Its Polar-to-Cartesian Geometry (PCG) backbone maps polar imaging-radar features into Cartesian voxels through fixed and deformable sampling, guiding cross-radar fusion for geometry and attribute prediction. Single-chip detection outputs provide class evidence, while raw Doppler spectra supply motion features and radial-velocity candidates. The velocity readout selects from these candidates using fused features to resolve aliasing, then combines the selected radial estimate with learned motion. Ego-motion compensation uses radar-estimated velocity, so inference requires no external odometry or other sensors. On K-Radar, single-frame PCG achieves 40.7% mIoU within 12.8 m, compared with RadarOcc's reported 34.3%. On the BRIDGE-Liv dataset, compared with a cascaded-radar baseline predicting the same outputs with external ego velocity, RadarOSV improves macro-averaged accuracy across four dynamic object classes within annotated object regions from 63.1% to 75.5% and reduces object radial-velocity MAE against manual Doppler annotations from 1.03 to 0.51 m/s, while maintaining geometric occupancy mIoU.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SF-Flow: Spectral Flow Matching with High Structural Fidelity for Hallucination-Suppressed Scientific Image Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Scientific image generation focuses on reproducing experimental appearance while following a prescribed spatial layout. A key challenge is acute data sparsity, which requires operating with unpaired collections of materials (real images and prescribed layouts), where no direct supervision is feasible. Work on unpaired translation has shown that it is possible to reproduce the texture and intensity variations of real images, but it is extremely hard to retain the intended phase boundaries in the prescribed locations. This paper tackles this challenge and introduces SF-Flow, a flow-matching model trained only on real material images that imposes spectral constraints during generation, producing images that are high-fidelity and consistent with the prescribed layouts. Because layouts enter only at generation time, the approach extends to layout maps outside the distribution of any available training layouts. We evaluate the method on synchrotron tomography of concrete, lens-coupled laboratory microCT of powders, and industrial XCT of additively manufactured metal. Without instrument-specific modeling, we show that SF-Flow achieves substantially higher template agreement and joint fidelity--structure score than previous methods, including contrastive unpaired translation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SalivaryHSI-Seg: A New Challenging Benchmark for Ex Vivo Salivary Gland Hyperspectral Tissue Segmentation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Salivary gland tumors are common lesions in oral and maxillofacial practice, and accurate identification of tumor regions and surrounding salivary gland tissues is important for tissue assessment, pathological sampling, and clinical decision support. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) records continuous spectral responses together with spatial imaging information, providing a promising way to capture fine-grained tissue-discriminative information. Nevertheless, the development of salivary gland HSI tissue segmentation remains limited due to the lack of standardized benchmarks with pixel-level annotations and unified evaluation protocols. To address this issue, we introduce SalivaryHSI-Seg, a hyperspectral tissue segmentation benchmark for ex vivo salivary gland specimens, containing 119 HSI samples from 31 patients with multi-class pixel-level annotations. We establish a patient-level five-fold cross-validation protocol and evaluate different input representations, model architectures, and challenging subsets with small tumor and complex boundary. Based on this benchmark, we further propose HyBSD, a hyperspectral boundary-guided spectral-difference network for full-HSI salivary gland tissue segmentation. HyBSD exploits boundary-guided spectral-difference cues to improve tissue delineation in ambiguous transition regions. Extensive experiments show that full-HSI input provides more discriminative information than sampled spectrums, and that HyBSD achieves 74.97% mDice and 87.76% Tumor Dice, with further advantages on the challenging subsets. Dataset and code will be released.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Pixel as the Common Language: Unified Multimodal Embedding via Visual Rendering
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multimodal embedding models map heterogeneous inputs into a shared representation space, yet text-only, image-only, and composed inputs are still presented in distinct formats and follow different routes through the model. This fragmentation prevents heterogeneous tasks from jointly optimizing the same end-to-end encoding process, limiting supervision transfer across input configurations. To address this issue, we propose unification before encoding and instantiate this paradigm in RenderEmbed. The framework uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert heterogeneous inputs into a common visual substrate for encoding with a VLM. From the resulting visual tokens, Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding produces compact retrieval representations by interleaving learnable anchors and fusing their states across layers, retaining broad context and fine-grained cues. Interventional Rendering Learning trains these representations to remain sensitive to content changes and stable across rendering variations through complementary semantic and rendering interventions. Extensive experiments on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, spanning diverse retrieval tasks, show that RenderEmbed outperforms prior state-of-the-art models at the same scale and exhibits strong out-of-domain generalization. Compared with MetaEmbed, RenderEmbed improves MMEB Overall Precision@1 by 1.7 points, with a larger 2.1-point gain on out-of-domain tasks. Transfer and scaling analyses further show that a shared visual pathway enables more effective learning from heterogeneous supervision.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: FolioWeaver: A LayerGraph-Grounded Agent for Layered Image Generation and Editing
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Layered image generation separates images into compositable layers, allowing users to manipulate individual elements independently. However, such asset-level editability does not enable the generation system to interpret successive feedback, perform targeted edits, and preserve unaffected content. We introduce FolioWeaver, a LayerGraph-grounded agent that unifies layered-image generation and iterative editing through a persistent Executable Scene State. FolioWeaver constructs a LayerGraph and generates independent visual assets conditioned on a shared scene reference. An Editing Agent performs feedback-driven modifications and self-repair through scoped actions, selective layer execution, and visual verification, enabling targeted updates while reusing unchanged assets. We also publicly release LayerFolio, a dataset of 100,377 human-reviewed layered scenes spanning six visual domains, together with two evaluation protocols: AtomicQA for measuring requirement satisfaction and CBLP for assessing layer organization. Experiments demonstrate that FolioWeaver achieves superior layer organization and composite fidelity compared with direct layered-generation methods. Analyses validate the contributions of component adaptation, execution-grounded repair, and cross-domain training. FolioWeaver advances layered-image generation toward persistent, controllable, and iterative visual creation. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/FolioWeaver/LayerFolio.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: WordEval: Evaluating Word-Native Operation Fidelity in Document Editing
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Microsoft Word is a central environment for office automation, and the faithful execution of its editing operations is an important capability for document agents. Unlike plain-text editing, editing in Word modifies a structured object model, where the requested effect is realized in object properties. Existing benchmarks, however, evaluate office workflows or desktop automation, treating word-processor documents as one task domain among many and verifying outcomes with keyword matching, per-task property checks, or screenshot comparison. We introduce WordEval, an operation-fidelity benchmark that instead centers evaluation on Word editing operations, testing whether each requested edit is realized as intended changes to Word objects and properties. It contains 642 cases across 15 Word feature areas, ranging from text and lists to charts, shape geometry, and SmartArt. 546 atomic cases cover 231 commands, 96 compositional cases combine multiple edits in a single document, and a Word-native oracle checks task-specific object properties and preservation conditions. Cases are constructed from editing-unit specifications, yielding controlled input documents, reference documents, and aligned oracle checks. Each compositional case is linked to corresponding atomic cases, supporting fine-grained diagnosis of editing failures. We evaluate eight agent systems and find that many struggle on the Atomic track, with performance varying across feature areas. Moreover, every system scores lower on Compositional than on Atomic, with gaps that vary substantially by system. Exact atomic-intent links and recorded failure diagnoses provide complementary views of this variation.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). Project page with code and data at https://aka.ms/word-eval

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Regularizing Hard Examples Improves Adversarial Robustness
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent studies have validated that pruning hard-to-learn examples from training improves the generalization performance of neural networks (NNs). In this study, we investigate this intriguing phenomenon -- the negative effect of hard examples on generalization -- in adversarial training. Particularly, we theoretically demonstrate that the increase in the difficulty of hard examples in adversarial training is significantly greater than the increase in the difficulty of easy examples. Furthermore, we verify that hard examples are only fitted through memorization of the label in adversarial training. We conduct both theoretical and empirical analyses of this memorization phenomenon, showing that pruning hard examples in adversarial training can enhance the model's robustness. However, the challenge remains in finding the optimal threshold for removing hard examples that degrade robustness performance. Based upon these observations, we propose a new approach, difficulty proportional label smoothing (DPLS), to adaptively mitigate the negative effect of hard examples, thereby improving the adversarial robustness of NNs. Notably, our experimental result indicates that our method can successfully leverage hard examples while circumventing the negative effect.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 48 pages, 16 figures, 22 tables. Published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR)

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Mem-X: A Memory-Dependent Cross-Episode Benchmark for Vision-and-Language Navigation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.
